title: I made a music puzzle game solo with AI coding assistance. Here’s what it was good at and where I had to take over.
author: SalamanderEast7639
selftext:
I’m a solo dev, and my game Hearsay comes out on Steam on November 3. You restore a music archive by putting cut-up tape pieces back in order, and the shelf checks each row like Wordle: yellow means right recording, wrong spot. The old recordings are real Library of Congress archives from before 1926. I built it in Godot 4.6, and I used an AI coding assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) for nearly all of the programming.

Here’s where I drew the line: no AI art, music or voice. The art is purchased, the modern music is by human artists and credited in the game, and the story tapes are my own voice. I wanted AI on the parts players never see.

**Where it really helped:**

* **Tests.** It wrote headless test scripts for almost every system: saves, perks, the shelf check, the leaderboards. When it changed one thing and broke another, a test usually caught it before I ever opened the game. This saved an enormous amount of time for me as a father of 2 working a full time job. 
* **Release-only bugs.** My exported build kept crashing at launch, but the editor never did. From one crash report it worked out that the leaderboard card on the main menu was asking Steam for rankings. If you pressed Continue before Steam answered, the answer came back to a card that no longer existed. The editor only prints an error for that, while an exported build crashes. It fixed the bug and made the crash report save each step as it happens, so the next report shows exactly what the game was doing.
* **Licensing.** I gave it strict rules: CC0 or CC BY tracks only, no AI music, and no tracks that trigger Content ID. It checked every track against those rules, and I uploaded unlisted test videos to YouTube to confirm. One recording got blocked in some countries, so we swapped it out.
* **The boring stuff.** Captions for my story tapes, achievement wiring, performance checks with hundreds of tapes on the floor and some other stuff as well.

**Where I had to take over:**

* **Feel.** It can’t play the game. The hint that explains yellow and red went through three versions before one felt right, and each time I had to play it myself and say “no, this feels wrong.”I found telling the AI exactly what you want with a picture or screenshot made it go by a lot faster and it usually created a better product.
* **Playtesting.** My friends found things it never would have. One finished the demo in 25 minutes, and another pointed out a tutorial line that just said “F.” When I say the screenshots were key this is where that rang true. The AI had trouble seeing what was happening in game but when playtesters played it they could see everything and screenshotted it all. 
* **Rules it has to follow every time.** I keep a list: close Godot before it writes files, never touch the project settings file, don’t overwrite anything I changed after it last read it. It follows the list, but I had to write the list.

My takeaway: treat it like a fast programmer who has never played your game. It’s great at code, tests and digging through crash reports. Design and feel are still on you.

There’s a free demo on Steam if you want to see the result: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5274720/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5274720/)

Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
